analysis.one_liner: Lets severely disabled borrowers cancel private student loans and makes student loans dischargeable in bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after its introduction it sat in subcommittee until the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require private lenders to cancel a student loan when the borrower becomes permanently and totally disabled, and it would make that cancellation tax-free so the forgiven debt would not count as income or as an asset for federal benefit programs. It would also end the special rule that makes student loans nearly impossible to wipe out in bankruptcy, returning them to ordinary treatment. The bill was referred to three committees and then to a subcommittee, where it stalled with no further action for the rest of the two-year Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Student borrowers with private loans who become permanently and totally disabled, including veterans rated unemployable due to a service-connected condition, would have their loans canceled tax-free. Borrowers crushed by student debt who file for bankruptcy would regain the ability to have their loans discharged like any other debt. Cosigners—often parents—would no longer face automatic default on a loan because of a cosigner's disability.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Disabled and heavily indebted student borrowers

how_it_helps.text: Requires private lenders to discharge a private education loan when the borrower is permanently and totally disabled, using the Education Department's existing disability standards or a VA determination of unemployability from a service-connected condition [S2] [S3].

Makes that discharge tax-free and excludes it from income or resources when calculating eligibility for federal and federally funded state benefit programs, so a disabled borrower would not face a surprise tax bill or lose disability benefits [S3].

Strikes the bankruptcy-code provision that shields student loans from discharge, so student loans could be wiped out in bankruptcy like credit card or medical debt instead of requiring proof of 'undue hardship' [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private student lenders would bear the cost: they would lose the ability to collect from borrowers with permanent total disabilities and would lose the special protection that makes student loans survive bankruptcy, likely pricing that risk into future loans or tightening underwriting.

drawbacks.text: Removing bankruptcy protection for all student loans could raise interest rates or tighten credit standards for future borrowers, since lenders would price in the chance that debts get wiped out in bankruptcy [S3].

The disability-discharge requirement applies only to private education loan agreements entered into 180 days or more after enactment, so borrowers with existing loans would not benefit from that provision [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are targeted and significant: borrowers with permanent disabilities and borrowers in genuine financial collapse are the people least able to pay. The main cost—somewhat higher rates or stricter lending on private student loans—falls on future borrowers as a group and is the honest tradeoff of restoring normal bankruptcy rights. On balance the bill helps the people with the least ability to pay at a modest, diffuse cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three committees, then to a Financial Services subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dan Kildee introduced the bill on February 18, 2021, joined by six Democratic cosponsors: Reps. Carson, Cohen, Dean, Norton, Perlmutter, and Vargas [S3] [S5].
The bill was referred the same day to the Financial Services, Judiciary, and Ways and Means Committees [S5].
In April 2021 it was referred to the Financial Services Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law, and that was the last recorded action [S5].
No further action—no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote—appears in the record before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student lenders keep the protections the bill would have removed: they can still collect from permanently disabled borrowers and student debts still survive bankruptcy, because the bill never advanced.

industries.note: The bill would require lenders to cancel loans for permanently and totally disabled borrowers and would let student debts be wiped out in bankruptcy, ending protections that let lenders collect from borrowers who cannot work. Lenders' interest in keeping those collection rights runs directly against disabled and insolvent borrowers.

industries.industry: Debt collectors and loan servicers for private student loans
industries.note: Loans discharged for disability or in bankruptcy could no longer be pursued for payment, shrinking the pool of debts available to collect on.
